items.text: It all starts with one word: equity. That's just the slice of the house you actually own — what it's worth, minus what you still owe. Say you put eighty thousand down on a four-hundred-thousand-dollar home; on day one, you own eighty thousand of it outright. Keep paying, or watch prices in the neighborhood climb, and that slice keeps widening. After a few years it can be real money — though it's tied up in the house, not cash in hand.

You get at that money by borrowing against it — you take out a brand-new loan, and the equity you've built sets the ceiling on how big it can be. You can do this whenever you like: years into the mortgage, or the day you buy. And it doesn't disturb the loan you already have. Your first mortgage stays exactly as it is. The new loan differs in just one way — who gets paid back first. If the home ever got sold to cover its debts, the first mortgage is paid in full before this new loan sees a single dollar. Since it only collects what's left over, we call it a second lien. And "second" there means second in line to be paid, not second in time. That lower spot in line is riskier for the lender, so a second lien usually costs a little more.

Most second liens come in one of two shapes. Either you take the whole amount in one piece — a fixed loan you pay off on a set schedule, which is a home-equity loan. Or you open a line you can draw from as you go, paying it down and borrowing again, a lot like a credit card, except here the house is what's backing it — that's a home-equity line. And one more thing: a buyer short on the down payment can set one up the very day they close, and use it to skip mortgage insurance. We'll come back to that.

Take the home-equity loan first. The lender hands over the whole amount at once, and everything is fixed: one lump sum, a set rate, and the same monthly payment for the life of the loan — steady and predictable, just like your first mortgage, only sitting behind it. It's what's called closed-end: once that money is paid out, that's the loan. Paying it down doesn't open anything back up to borrow again. So it is perfect when you know the exact number you need up front — a specific renovation, say, or rolling a few fixed debts into one payment. When the need is more open-ended, the line of credit is the better fit.

A home-equity line — a hee-lock — stays open for about ten years. That stretch is called the draw period, and during it you can pull money out and pay it back as often as you like. Usually you're only billed interest on whatever you're carrying at the moment, at a rate that rides along with the Prime rate — so it moves up and down with the market. Once the draw period ends, the line freezes: no more borrowing, and whatever balance is left gets paid off over the years that remain.

Now, second liens tie into a real money-saving move at purchase. On a conventional loan, if you put less than twenty percent down, the lender tacks on private mortgage insurance — P-M-I — a monthly charge that protects the lender if you default, and does absolutely nothing for you. But here's the detail that matters: P-M-I is tied to the first mortgage alone, and it only kicks in once that first mortgage climbs above eighty percent of the home's value.

So a buyer with only ten percent to put down has a clever way around it: split the financing into two loans instead of one big mortgage. Let's use a three-hundred-thousand-dollar home. One single mortgage would be two hundred seventy thousand — that's ninety percent of the value, above the eighty-percent line, so P-M-I kicks in. Instead, the buyer takes a first mortgage for exactly eighty percent of the value — two hundred forty thousand — then adds a second lien for the next thirty thousand, and puts thirty thousand, ten percent, down. Now the first mortgage sits right at eighty percent, so no P-M-I, and that little second lien fills the gap. Lenders call this pairing a piggyback, and they name it by its pieces — this one is an eighty-ten-ten: eighty percent first, ten percent second, ten percent down.
